data.turoyo: Maḥšamme. Mparqaʕ u ʕafd. Qayəmle Kandar, pažele bas sayfe.
data.translation: Als sie nun gegessen hatten, brach der Riese zusammen; Kander ging auf ihn los und hieb ihn mit seinem Schwert in Stücke.

rationale: Second Detransitive Preterit example; animate subject collapses/bursts after eating, contrasting with cooked grain.

data.turoyo: I naqqa d axəlle, mḥela u tarwoḏayḏa i kačke, hawyo tleṯi pižat, əmmo palaq, mparqaʕla.
data.translation: Als sie nun aßen, und sie einen Löffel voll in den Mund nahm, ging das Mädchen in dreißig stücke, "Bautz!" Es platzte.

rationale: Second active Preterit example gives feminine l-series subject in intransitive bursting.

summary: The active Preterit mparqaʕle/mparqaʕla has l-series subjects but denotes intransitive bursting. Detransitive mparqaʕ/mparqʕo is not defined simply by absence of a semantic causer.
JL 17.5/5 miparqʕo is Infectum, embedded in past cooking discourse; JL 17.5/6 mparqʕo is completed/result-state Preterit. Preserve that contrast.
The supplied PrS 10/32 German says the ogre collapsed before Kandar cut him into pieces. Do not use the latter action to claim the verb itself means cutting to pieces.
Does PrS 10/32 Mparqaʕ mean an actual bodily burst or collapse without rupture? One context supports only a cautious extension, not a separate lexical sense.
What conditions the l-series intransitive Preterit versus Detransitive forms for bursting in animate subjects?

rationale: The supplied edition translation of JL 17.5/6 reads "unser gekochter Weizen". The entry omits the i in Weizen.

summary: Subjects include grain, a kitten, a girl, an ogre and a building. The event may be induced by eating, heating or exertion without an expressed agent in the Detransitive clause.
